/-!
# Conjecture 7.25

by A. V. Kuznetsov

We associate with words in the alphabet $x, x^{-1}, y, y^{-1}, z, z^{-1}, \ldots$ operations
which are understood as functions in the variables $x, y, z, \ldots$. A word $A$ is
*expressible in words $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ on the group $G$* if $A$ can be constructed from
the words $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ and variables by means of finitely many substitutions of words
one into another and replacements of a word by another word which is identically equal to it
on $G$. A list of words is *functionally complete on $G$* if every word can be expressed on
$G$ in words from this list. A word $B$ is a *Schaeffer word on $G$* if every word can be
expressed on $G$ in $B$.

Does there exist an algorithm which decides

- a) by a word $B$, whether it is a Schaeffer word on every group?
  (Examples of such words: $xy^{-1}$, $x^{-1}y^2z$, $x^{-1}y^{-1}zx$.)
- b) by a list of words, whether it is functionally complete on every group?
- c) by words $A, B_1, \ldots, B_n$, whether $A$ is expressible in $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ on every
  group?
- d) the same for every finite group? (For finite groups, for example, $x^{-1}$ is expressible
  in $xy$.) For a fixed finite group an algorithm exists.

In this file a word is a list of letters $x_i^{\pm 1}$, encoded as pairs `(i, b)` with
`b = true` for $x_i$ and `b = false` for $x_i^{-1}$; this is the word representation used by
`FreeGroup`. Substitution of words into a word replaces each letter $x_i$ by the word
substituted for $x_i$ and each letter $x_i^{-1}$ by the formal inverse of that word, so that
it corresponds to composition of the associated functions (`Word.eval_subst`). The
quantifier over the group $G$ is placed outside expressibility: the construction of $A$, and
the identities of $G$ that it uses, may depend on $G$. The existence of an algorithm is
formalised as `ComputablePred`.

*References:*
- [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46), Problem 7.25
- A. V. Kuznetsov, *Matem. Issledovaniya*, Kishinëv, **6**, no. 4 (1971), 75–122 (Russian)
-/

inductive IsExpressibleOn (G : Type*) [Group G] (Bs : List Word) : Word → Prop
  /-- Each of the given words is expressible. -/
  | basic {B : Word} (hB : B ∈ Bs) : IsExpressibleOn G Bs B
  /-- Each variable is expressible. -/
  | var (i : ℕ) : IsExpressibleOn G Bs (Word.var i)
  /-- Substituting expressible words into an expressible word gives an expressible word. -/
  | subst {W : Word} (σ : ℕ → Word) (hW : IsExpressibleOn G Bs W)
      (hσ : ∀ i, IsExpressibleOn G Bs (σ i)) : IsExpressibleOn G Bs (W.subst σ)
  /-- A word identically equal on `G` to an expressible word is expressible. -/
  | replace {W W' : Word} (hW : IsExpressibleOn G Bs W) (h : Word.IdenticallyEqualOn G W W') :
      IsExpressibleOn G Bs W'
blocks.docstring:
`IsExpressibleOn G Bs A` says that the word `A` is expressible in the words of the list
`Bs` on the group `G`: `A` can be constructed from the words in `Bs` and the variables by
finitely many substitutions of words one into another and replacements of a word by
another word which is identically equal to it on `G`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: Subgroup.closure / Submonoid.closure (wrong kind of closure: not closed under substitution); Mathlib has no clone theory.
justification.name: Kourovka.«7.25».IsExpressibleOn
justification.why_needed: Kuznetsov's expressibility: inductive closure of the given words and the variables under substitution and replacement by identically equal words on G. Nothing on clones / functional completeness / term-operation closure exists in Mathlib or FormalConjecturesForMathlib.

blocks.name: IsExpressibleOn
blocks.text:
/-- `IsExpressibleOn G Bs A` says that the word `A` is expressible in the words of the list
`Bs` on the group `G`: `A` can be constructed from the words in `Bs` and the variables by
finitely many substitutions of words one into another and replacements of a word by
another word which is identically equal to it on `G`. -/
inductive IsExpressibleOn (G : Type*) [Group G] (Bs : List Word) : Word → Prop
  /-- Each of the given words is expressible. -/
  | basic {B : Word} (hB : B ∈ Bs) : IsExpressibleOn G Bs B
  /-- Each variable is expressible. -/
  | var (i : ℕ) : IsExpressibleOn G Bs (Word.var i)
  /-- Substituting expressible words into an expressible word gives an expressible word. -/
  | subst {W : Word} (σ : ℕ → Word) (hW : IsExpressibleOn G Bs W)
      (hσ : ∀ i, IsExpressibleOn G Bs (σ i)) : IsExpressibleOn G Bs (W.subst σ)
  /-- A word identically equal on `G` to an expressible word is expressible. -/
  | replace {W W' : Word} (hW : IsExpressibleOn G Bs W) (h : Word.IdenticallyEqualOn G W W') :
      IsExpressibleOn G Bs W'

def IsFunctionallyCompleteOn (G : Type*) [Group G] (Bs : List Word) : Prop :=
  ∀ A : Word, IsExpressibleOn G Bs A
blocks.docstring:
A list of words `Bs` is functionally complete on the group `G` if every word is
expressible in the words of `Bs` on `G`.

justification.name: Kourovka.«7.25».IsFunctionallyCompleteOn, Kourovka.«7.25».IsSchaefferWordOn
justification.why_needed: Direct transcriptions of 'functionally complete on G' (every word expressible in the list) and 'Schaeffer word on G' (functionally complete singleton list).

blocks.name: IsFunctionallyCompleteOn

/-- A list of words `Bs` is functionally complete on the group `G` if every word is
expressible in the words of `Bs` on `G`. -/
def IsFunctionallyCompleteOn (G : Type*) [Group G] (Bs : List Word) : Prop :=
  ∀ A : Word, IsExpressibleOn G Bs A

def IsSchaefferWordOn (G : Type*) [Group G] (B : Word) : Prop :=
  IsFunctionallyCompleteOn G [B]

@[category API, AMS 8 20]
theorem Word.eval_subst (w : Word) (σ : ℕ → Word) (v : ℕ → G) :
    (w.subst σ).eval v = w.eval fun i => (σ i).eval v := by
  induction w with
  | nil => simp [Word.eval, Word.subst, FreeGroup.lift_mk]
  | cons l w ih =>
    obtain ⟨i, b⟩ := l
    rw [Word.subst, List.flatMap_cons, Word.eval_append, ← Word.subst, ih]
    cases b
    · rw [cond_false, Word.eval_invRev]
      simp [Word.eval, FreeGroup.lift_mk]
    · simp [Word.eval, FreeGroup.lift_mk]

@[category test, AMS 8 20]
theorem isSchaefferWordOn_xyinv (G : Type*) [Group G] :
    IsSchaefferWordOn G [(0, true), (1, false)] := by
  set B : Word := [(0, true), (1, false)] with hBdef
  have hB : IsExpressibleOn G [B] B := .basic (List.mem_singleton_self B)
  -- the empty word: $xx^{-1} = 1$
  have hone : IsExpressibleOn G [B] [] := by
    refine .replace (.subst (fun _ => Word.var 0) hB fun _ => .var 0) fun v => ?_
    simp [Word.eval, Word.subst, Word.var, FreeGroup.invRev, FreeGroup.lift_mk, hBdef]
  -- $x^{-1}$: substitute the empty word for $x$ and $x$ for $y$ in $xy^{-1}$
  have hinv : IsExpressibleOn G [B] [(0, false)] := by
    have := IsExpressibleOn.subst (fun i => if i = 0 then [] else Word.var 0) hB
      fun i => by dsimp only; split_ifs <;> [exact hone; exact .var 0]
    exact this
  -- $y^{-1}$
  have hinv1 : IsExpressibleOn G [B] [(1, false)] :=
    IsExpressibleOn.subst (fun _ => Word.var 1) hinv fun _ => .var 1
  -- $xy$: substitute $y^{-1}$ for $y$ in $xy^{-1}$
  have hxy : IsExpressibleOn G [B] [(0, true), (1, true)] := by
    have := IsExpressibleOn.subst (fun i => if i = 0 then Word.var 0 else [(1, false)]) hB
      fun i => by dsimp only; split_ifs <;> [exact .var 0; exact hinv1]
    exact this
  -- $x^{-1}y$: substitute $x^{-1}$ for $x$ and $y^{-1}$ for $y$ in $xy^{-1}$
  have hxinvy : IsExpressibleOn G [B] [(0, false), (1, true)] := by
    have := IsExpressibleOn.subst (fun i => if i = 0 then [(0, false)] else [(1, false)]) hB
      fun i => by dsimp only; split_ifs <;> [exact hinv; exact hinv1]
    exact this
  intro w
  induction w with
  | nil => exact hone
  | cons l w ih =>
    obtain ⟨i, b⟩ := l
    cases b
    · have := IsExpressibleOn.subst (fun j => if j = 0 then Word.var i else w) hxinvy
        fun j => by dsimp only; split_ifs <;> [exact .var i; exact ih]
      simpa [Word.subst, Word.var, FreeGroup.invRev] using this
    · have := IsExpressibleOn.subst (fun j => if j = 0 then Word.var i else w) hxy
        fun j => by dsimp only; split_ifs <;> [exact .var i; exact ih]
      simpa [Word.subst, Word.var] using this

  -- $x^{-1}$: substitute the empty word for $x$ and $x$ for $y$ in $xy^{-1}$
  have hinv : IsExpressibleOn G [B] [(0, false)] := by
    have := IsExpressibleOn.subst (fun i => if i = 0 then [] else Word.var 0) hB
      fun i => by dsimp only; split_ifs <;> [exact hone; exact .var 0]
    exact this
  -- $y^{-1}$

    IsExpressibleOn.subst (fun _ => Word.var 1) hinv fun _ => .var 1
  -- $xy$: substitute $y^{-1}$ for $y$ in $xy^{-1}$
  have hxy : IsExpressibleOn G [B] [(0, true), (1, true)] := by
    have := IsExpressibleOn.subst (fun i => if i = 0 then Word.var 0 else [(1, false)]) hB
      fun i => by dsimp only; split_ifs <;> [exact .var 0; exact hinv1]
    exact this
  -- $x^{-1}y$: substitute $x^{-1}$ for $x$ and $y^{-1}$ for $y$ in $xy^{-1}$
  have hxinvy : IsExpressibleOn G [B] [(0, false), (1, true)] := by
    have := IsExpressibleOn.subst (fun i => if i = 0 then [(0, false)] else [(1, false)]) hB
      fun i => by dsimp only; split_ifs <;> [exact hinv; exact hinv1]
    exact this
  intro w
  induction w with
  | nil => exact hone
  | cons l w ih =>
    obtain ⟨i, b⟩ := l
    cases b
    · have := IsExpressibleOn.subst (fun j => if j = 0 then Word.var i else w) hxinvy
        fun j => by dsimp only; split_ifs <;> [exact .var i; exact ih]
      simpa [Word.subst, Word.var, FreeGroup.invRev] using this
    · have := IsExpressibleOn.subst (fun j => if j = 0 then Word.var i else w) hxy
        fun j => by dsimp only; split_ifs <;> [exact .var i; exact ih]
      simpa [Word.subst, Word.var] using this

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 7.25

by A. V. Kuznetsov

We associate with words in the alphabet $x, x^{-1}, y, y^{-1}, z, z^{-1}, \ldots$ operations
which are understood as functions in the variables $x, y, z, \ldots$. A word $A$ is
*expressible in words $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ on the group $G$* if $A$ can be constructed from
the words $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ and variables by means of finitely many substitutions of words
one into another and replacements of a word by another word which is identically equal to it
on $G$. A list of words is *functionally complete on $G$* if every word can be expressed on
$G$ in words from this list. A word $B$ is a *Schaeffer word on $G$* if every word can be
expressed on $G$ in $B$.

Does there exist an algorithm which decides

- a) by a word $B$, whether it is a Schaeffer word on every group?
  (Examples of such words: $xy^{-1}$, $x^{-1}y^2z$, $x^{-1}y^{-1}zx$.)
- b) by a list of words, whether it is functionally complete on every group?
- c) by words $A, B_1, \ldots, B_n$, whether $A$ is expressible in $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ on every
  group?
- d) the same for every finite group? (For finite groups, for example, $x^{-1}$ is expressible
  in $xy$.) For a fixed finite group an algorithm exists.

In this file a word is a list of letters $x_i^{\pm 1}$, encoded as pairs `(i, b)` with
`b = true` for $x_i$ and `b = false` for $x_i^{-1}$; this is the word representation used by
`FreeGroup`. Substitution of words into a word replaces each letter $x_i$ by the word
substituted for $x_i$ and each letter $x_i^{-1}$ by the formal inverse of that word, so that
it corresponds to composition of the associated functions (`Word.eval_subst`). The
quantifier over the group $G$ is placed outside expressibility: the construction of $A$, and
the identities of $G$ that it uses, may depend on $G$. The existence of an algorithm is
formalised as `ComputablePred`.

*References:*
- [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46), Problem 7.25
- A. V. Kuznetsov, *Matem. Issledovaniya*, Kishinëv, **6**, no. 4 (1971), 75–122 (Russian)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«7.25»

/-- A word in the alphabet $x_0, x_0^{-1}, x_1, x_1^{-1}, \ldots$: a list of letters
`(i, b)`, where `(i, true)` stands for $x_i$ and `(i, false)` for $x_i^{-1}$. -/
abbrev Word : Type := List (ℕ × Bool)

/-- The word consisting of the single letter $x_i$. -/
def Word.var (i : ℕ) : Word := [(i, true)]

/-- The function on a group `G` associated with a word: the value of the word `w` at the
assignment `v` of elements of `G` to the variables. -/
def Word.eval {G : Type*} [Group G] (w : Word) (v : ℕ → G) : G :=
  FreeGroup.lift v (FreeGroup.mk w)

/-- Substitution of the words `σ i` for the variables $x_i$ in the word `w`: every letter
$x_i$ is replaced by `σ i` and every letter $x_i^{-1}$ by the formal inverse of `σ i`. -/
def Word.subst (w : Word) (σ : ℕ → Word) : Word :=
  w.flatMap fun l => cond l.2 (σ l.1) (FreeGroup.invRev (σ l.1))

/-- Two words are identically equal on the group `G` if they define the same function
on `G`. -/
def Word.IdenticallyEqualOn (G : Type*) [Group G] (w w' : Word) : Prop :=
  ∀ v : ℕ → G, w.eval v = w'.eval v

/-- `IsExpressibleOn G Bs A` says that the word `A` is expressible in the words of the list
`Bs` on the group `G`: `A` can be constructed from the words in `Bs` and the variables by
finitely many substitutions of words one into another and replacements of a word by
another word which is identically equal to it on `G`. -/
inductive IsExpressibleOn (G : Type*) [Group G] (Bs : List Word) : Word → Prop
  /-- Each of the given words is expressible. -/
  | basic {B : Word} (hB : B ∈ Bs) : IsExpressibleOn G Bs B
  /-- Each variable is expressible. -/
  | var (i : ℕ) : IsExpressibleOn G Bs (Word.var i)
  /-- Substituting expressible words into an expressible word gives an expressible word. -/
  | subst {W : Word} (σ : ℕ → Word) (hW : IsExpressibleOn G Bs W)
      (hσ : ∀ i, IsExpressibleOn G Bs (σ i)) : IsExpressibleOn G Bs (W.subst σ)
  /-- A word identically equal on `G` to an expressible word is expressible. -/
  | replace {W W' : Word} (hW : IsExpressibleOn G Bs W) (h : Word.IdenticallyEqualOn G W W') :
      IsExpressibleOn G Bs W'

/-- A list of words `Bs` is functionally complete on the group `G` if every word is
expressible in the words of `Bs` on `G`. -/
def IsFunctionallyCompleteOn (G : Type*) [Group G] (Bs : List Word) : Prop :=
  ∀ A : Word, IsExpressibleOn G Bs A

/-- A word `B` is a Schaeffer word on the group `G` if every word is expressible in `B`
on `G`. -/
def IsSchaefferWordOn (G : Type*) [Group G] (B : Word) : Prop :=
  IsFunctionallyCompleteOn G [B]

section API

variable {G : Type*} [Group G]

/-- The function associated with the variable $x_i$ is the $i$-th projection. -/
@[category API, AMS 8 20]
theorem Word.eval_var (i : ℕ) (v : ℕ → G) : (Word.var i).eval v = v i := by
  simp [Word.eval, Word.var, FreeGroup.lift_mk]

/-- The function associated with a concatenation is the product of the functions. -/
@[category API, AMS 8 20]
theorem Word.eval_append (w₁ w₂ : Word) (v : ℕ → G) :
    (w₁ ++ w₂).eval v = w₁.eval v * w₂.eval v := by
  simp [Word.eval, ← FreeGroup.mul_mk]

/-- The function associated with the formal inverse of a word is the inverse of the
function. -/
@[category API, AMS 8 20]
theorem Word.eval_invRev (w : Word) (v : ℕ → G) :
    Word.eval (FreeGroup.invRev w) v = (w.eval v)⁻¹ := by
  rw [Word.eval, Word.eval, ← FreeGroup.inv_mk, map_inv]

/-- Substitution of words into a word corresponds to composition of the associated
functions. -/
@[category API, AMS 8 20]
theorem Word.eval_subst (w : Word) (σ : ℕ → Word) (v : ℕ → G) :
    (w.subst σ).eval v = w.eval fun i => (σ i).eval v := by
  induction w with
  | nil => simp [Word.eval, Word.subst, FreeGroup.lift_mk]
  | cons l w ih =>
    obtain ⟨i, b⟩ := l
    rw [Word.subst, List.flatMap_cons, Word.eval_append, ← Word.subst, ih]
    cases b
    · rw [cond_false, Word.eval_invRev]
      simp [Word.eval, FreeGroup.lift_mk]
    · simp [Word.eval, FreeGroup.lift_mk]

end API

/--
Does there exist an algorithm which decides, by a word $B$, whether it is a Schaeffer word on
every group?

That is, is the set of words $B$ such that $B$ is a Schaeffer word on every group $G$ a
computable predicate on words? Examples of words which are Schaeffer words on every group are
$xy^{-1}$, $x^{-1}y^2z$ and $x^{-1}y^{-1}zx$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 8 20]
theorem kourovka.«7.25».parts.a : answer(sorry) ↔
    ComputablePred fun B : Word => ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], IsSchaefferWordOn G B := by
  sorry

/--
Does there exist an algorithm which decides, by a list of words $B_1, \ldots, B_n$, whether
it is functionally complete on every group?

That is, is the set of lists of words $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ such that $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ is
functionally complete on every group $G$ a computable predicate on lists of words?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 8 20]
theorem kourovka.«7.25».parts.b : answer(sorry) ↔
    ComputablePred fun Bs : List Word =>
      ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], IsFunctionallyCompleteOn G Bs := by
  sorry

/--
Does there exist an algorithm which decides, by words $A, B_1, \ldots, B_n$, whether $A$ is
expressible in $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ on every group?

That is, is the set of pairs $(A, (B_1, \ldots, B_n))$ such that $A$ is expressible in
$B_1, \ldots, B_n$ on every group $G$ a computable predicate on such pairs? This is a problem from
A. V. Kuznetsov, *Matem. Issledovaniya* **6**, no. 4 (1971), p. 112.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 8 20]
theorem kourovka.«7.25».parts.c : answer(sorry) ↔
    ComputablePred fun p : Word × List Word =>
      ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], IsExpressibleOn G p.2 p.1 := by
  sorry

/--
Does there exist an algorithm which decides, by words $A, B_1, \ldots, B_n$, whether $A$ is
expressible in $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ on every finite group?

That is, is the set of pairs $(A, (B_1, \ldots, B_n))$ such that $A$ is expressible in
$B_1, \ldots, B_n$ on every finite group $G$ a computable predicate on such pairs? The
construction of $A$ may depend on the finite group $G$: for example, $x^{-1}$ is expressible
in $xy$ on every finite group, as $x^{-1} = x^{|G|-1}$ on $G$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 8 20]
theorem kourovka.«7.25».parts.d : answer(sorry) ↔
    ComputablePred fun p : Word × List Word =>
      ∀ (G : Type) [Group G] [Finite G], IsExpressibleOn G p.2 p.1 := by
  sorry

      simpa [Word.subst, Word.var, FreeGroup.invRev] using this
    · have := IsExpressibleOn.subst (fun j => if j = 0 then Word.var i else w) hxy
        fun j => by dsimp only; split_ifs <;> [exact .var i; exact ih]
      simpa [Word.subst, Word.var] using this

/-- On every finite group $G$, the word $x^{-1}$ is expressible in $xy$, since
$x^{-1} = x^{2|G|-1}$ on $G$. This is the example given in part d) of the problem. -/
@[category test, AMS 8 20]
theorem isExpressibleOn_inv_of_finite (G : Type*) [Group G] [Finite G] :
    IsExpressibleOn G [[(0, true), (1, true)]] [(0, false)] := by
  set B : Word := [(0, true), (1, true)] with hBdef
  have hB : IsExpressibleOn G [B] B := .basic (List.mem_singleton_self B)
  -- the powers $x^{k+1}$ are expressible in $xy$
  have hpow : ∀ k, IsExpressibleOn G [B] (List.replicate (k + 1) (0, true)) := by
    intro k
    induction k with
    | zero => exact .var 0
    | succ k ih =>
      have := IsExpressibleOn.subst (fun i => if i = 0 then List.replicate (k + 1) (0, true)
        else Word.var 0) hB fun i => by dsimp only; split_ifs <;> [exact ih; exact .var 0]
      simpa [Word.subst, Word.var, hBdef, List.replicate_succ'] using this
  have hcard : 1 ≤ Nat.card G := Nat.one_le_iff_ne_zero.mpr Nat.card_pos.ne'
  refine .replace (hpow (2 * Nat.card G - 2)) fun v => ?_
  have h2 : 2 * Nat.card G - 2 + 1 = 2 * Nat.card G - 1 := by omega
  simp only [Word.eval, FreeGroup.lift_mk, List.map_replicate, List.prod_replicate, h2,
    List.map_cons, List.map_nil, List.prod_cons, List.prod_nil, mul_one]
  simp only [cond_true, cond_false]
  apply eq_inv_of_mul_eq_one_left
  rw [← pow_succ, Nat.sub_add_cancel (by omega), pow_mul, pow_card_eq_one']

/-- On the infinite cyclic group, the empty word is not expressible in the empty list of
words: every word expressible in no words takes the value $1$ when all variables are set
to the generator $1 \in \mathbb{Z}$. -/
@[category test, AMS 8 20]
theorem not_isExpressibleOn_nil_nil :
    ¬ IsExpressibleOn (Multiplicative ℤ) [] [] := by
  have key : ∀ W, IsExpressibleOn (Multiplicative ℤ) [] W →
      W.eval (fun _ => Multiplicative.ofAdd (1 : ℤ)) = Multiplicative.ofAdd 1 := by
    intro W hW
    induction hW with
    | basic hB => simp at hB
    | var i => simp [Word.eval_var]
    | subst σ _ _ ih ihσ => rw [Word.eval_subst]; simp only [ihσ]; exact ih
    | replace _ h ih => rw [← h, ih]
  intro h
  have := key [] h
  simp only [Word.eval, FreeGroup.lift_mk, List.map_nil, List.prod_nil] at this
  exact one_ne_zero (ofAdd_eq_one.mp this.symm)

end Tests

items: Words are unreduced lists of letters (List (ℕ × Bool)) rather than FreeGroup elements. Since a word and its free reduction are identically equal on every group, and reduction/`FreeGroup.mk` are computable, the decidability questions are unaffected; this keeps the input of the algorithm literally 'a word'.

The substitution rule is simultaneous substitution σ : ℕ → Word into all variables, requiring every σ i to be expressible. Since variables are expressible, this contains single-variable substitution, and with infinitely many variables single substitutions plus renaming generate simultaneous ones, so the closure is the same as the notebook's 'finitely many substitutions of words one into another'.

Substituting a word U for x_i replaces letters x_i^{-1} by the formal inverse FreeGroup.invRev U; Word.eval_subst shows this equals composition of the associated functions, which is the intended meaning of substitution of operations.
'Identically equal on G' is ∀ v : ℕ → G, eval w v = eval w' v (assignments to all countably many variables; words depend on finitely many).

'On every group' is ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], outside the expressibility predicate (as in existing Kourovka files, which use Type). Restricting to universe 0 loses nothing: expressibility on G depends only on the identities of G, and every group has a countable group (the relatively free group of its variety on countably many generators) with the same identities.

'Does there exist an algorithm' is formalized as ComputablePred (Mathlib's computability theory) on Word, List Word and Word × List Word with the standard Primcodable instances; answer(True) means an algorithm exists.
Part d) is formalized only as the finite-group analogue of part c), as prescribed by the decomposition table; the finite-group analogues of a) and b) are not stated.
The empty word and the empty list of words are allowed as inputs (they are words / lists in the ordinary sense); this does not change the decidability questions.

Additional API lemmas (Word.eval_var/eval_append/eval_invRev/eval_subst) and tests (xy^{-1} is a Schaeffer word on every group; x^{-1} expressible in xy on every finite group; a negative example) are included with full proofs to validate the bespoke definitions, following the repository's request for basic API tests.

statement:
We associate with words in the alphabet $x$, $x^{-1}$, $y$, $y^{-1}$, $z$, $z^{-1},\ldots $ operations which are understood as functions in variables $x, y, z,\ldots $. We say that a word $A$ is expressible in words $B_1,\ldots ,B_n$ on the group $G$ if $A$ can be constructed from the words $B_1,\ldots ,B_n$ and variables by means of finitely many substitutions of words one into another and replacements of a word by another word which is identically equal to it on $G$. A list of words is said to be functionally complete on $G$ if every word can be expressed on $G$ in words from this list. A word $B$ is called a Schaeffer word on $G$ if every word can be expressed on $G$ in $B$ (compare with A. V. Kuznetsov, Matem. Issledovaniya, Kishinëv, 6, no. 4 (1971), 75–122 (Russian)). Does there exist an algorithm which decides

a) by a word $B$, whether it is a Schaeffer word on every group? Compare with the problem of describing all such words in (A. G. Kurosh, Theory of Groups, Moscow, Nauka, 1967, p. 435 (Russian)); here are examples of such words: $xy^{-1}$, $x^{-1}y^2z$, $x^{-1}y^{-1}zx$.

b) by a list of words, whether it is functionally complete on every group?

c) by words $A, B_1,\ldots ,B_n$, whether $A$ is expressible in $ B_1,\ldots ,B_n$ on every group? (This is a problem from A. V. Kuznetsov, ibid., p. 112.)

d) the same for every finite group? (For finite groups, for example, $x^{-1}$ is expressible in $xy$.) For a fixed finite group an algorithm exists (compare with A. V. Kuznetsov, ibid., $\S$ 8).
